tier_reason: The repository README names cppjieba only through link titles ('Optimizing jieba-rs to be 33% faster than cppjieba', 2019, by contributor Paul Meng); the post's host does not resolve here, so corpus, hardware and flags are unseen (snippet only). The only full table is first-party-adjacent binding numbers in the napi-rs/node-rs README whose current benchmark code no longer runs the nodejieba row, so nothing reaches A or B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README link title only: 'Optimizing jieba-rs to be 33% faster than cppjieba' (2019-06-30 post, unreachable here; a search snippet of the later 'Making jieba-rs 2.4x faster' post says only that 'back in 2019, Paul Meng wrote a post about getting jieba-rs 33% faster than cppjieba'). The 2.4x post is jieba-rs against its own earlier version (2.85 us to 1.32 us per call on the HMM path, Apple M4 Max, criterion, one sentence; snippet only). Related binding numbers in the napi-rs/node-rs packages/jieba README (jieba-rs 0.11.0 through @node-rs/jieba against nodejieba 3.5.8, which wraps cppjieba; Apple M4 Max, Node.js v26.8.2, tinybench): Cut on the 246,568-character weicheng text 17,941,189 ns vs 39,167,640 ns average, about 2.18x (derived from page data); Cut on the 1,184-character preface 61,311 ns vs 133,632 ns, about 2.18x (derived from page data); Tag 1,184 characters 158,515 ns vs 305,060 ns and Tag 246,568 characters 42,167,642 ns vs 86,278,741 ns, about 1.9-2.05x (derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: Title-only evidence for the cppjieba comparison: the 2019 blog host (blog.paulme.ng) and messense.me do not resolve from this environment, so the numbers, corpus, hardware and compiler flags are unverified, and the 2019 figure predates years of changes to both projects. The repository's examples/weicheng/src/main.rs mirrors cppjieba's load test (cut every line of the Weicheng novel 50 times with HMM) but installs tikv-jemallocator as the global allocator, while cppjieba's test/load_test.cpp uses the system allocator, clock() timing and now a different input (synthetic_doc.utf8); cppjieba's CMakeLists adds -O3 -g. The crate's own cargo bench (criterion/CodSpeed) measures jieba-rs only. The @node-rs/jieba README table (about 2.2x over nodejieba) goes through two different binding layers (N-API in Rust vs nodejieba's C++ addon), the README itself credits part of the gain to N-API being faster than the v8 C++ API, node-rs builds with lto=true and codegen-units=1 while nodejieba's build flags are not stated, and the current packages/jieba/benchmark/jieba.ts only adds the '@node-rs/jieba' row (nodejieba is no longer a dependency), so the comparison table cannot be regenerated from the repository. The 1,184 and 246,568 'words' in that table are JavaScript string lengths in characters. Kept as a lead for re-running cppjieba against current jieba-rs on the same corpus with the same allocator.

notes: Real port with a long-standing, widely relayed 33%-faster-than-cppjieba claim, but the only source with the number is an unreachable 2019 contributor blog; tier C (snippet/title only). Shortcomings: no reproducible cppjieba comparison in the repo, jemalloc vs system allocator in the mirrored load test, binding-level numbers in @node-rs/jieba confounded by N-API vs nodejieba binding and no longer reproducible from its bench script. Not a language-level claim; same jieba algorithm (prefix-dict DAG plus HMM Viterbi) on both sides but harness equivalence unverified.

tier_reason: README carries a first-party hyperfine run (cpp-baseline 505.4 ms, rs-baseline 145.2 ms, rs-prealloc 97.2 ms, 5.20 +/- 0.10x) on an AMD Ryzen 9 5900X, but the bench/ binaries and build commands are not in the repository and neither side's compiler flags are stated, so it cannot be A; the README's own 2026-02-25 update says the C++ project is now slightly faster.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README and the bench/ directory is not committed. The Rust author's GitLab issue #3 (2026-02-14) asks whether 'cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release . && make' is the proper optimized build, implying a Release build of the C++ side; the C++ CMakeLists.txt sets no default build type (C++20, OpenCASCADE linked), so a plain cmake build would carry no -O flag. Rust side: Cargo release defaults (no custom [profile.release]; dev/test dependency opt-level 2).
corrections.caveats: Superseded by the README's own update: after the C++ project changed, it is 'now slightly faster again than this Rust codebase', so the 5.2x figure is obsolete. The measured C++ baseline was the 2026-02-05 rewrite (GitLab commit fb5e2f81), which used libstdc++ std::regex for NUM_PATTERN, NAME_PATTERN, REF_PATTERN and UNCERTAINTY_PATTERN; commit 06fdbc67 on 2026-02-15 (the day after issue #3) replaced those regexes with hand-written parsing and also fixed a C++ correctness bug ('Missed an identity element ... led to some breakage in repeated patterns'), so the numbers were taken against baseline code later fixed for correctness. Single 1 MiB input file in a niche format (STEP CAD), hyperfine with 3 warmups; the gap is a std::regex-versus-regex-crate illustration, not a language result. The Rust port was produced with LLM help and the author disclaims correctness beyond the test suite. The original C++ project is on GitLab (sethhillbrand/stepreduce, GPL-3.0-or-later; GitLab reports no detected license object); its issue page carries embedded text addressed to AI agents, which was ignored.
corrections.why_faster: Text-matching engine, not the language: the C++ baseline ran libstdc++ std::regex for four patterns, while rs-baseline used the Rust regex crate (3.5x) and rs-find-numbers/rs-prealloc replaced the number regex with hand-written scanning (src/find_numbers.rs) and preallocated buffers (another 1.49x). The C++ project's own removal of std::regex on 2026-02-15 erased the gap, which supports this attribution.

notes: Real measurement but against a superseded C++ version; flag as not faster any more (README update 2026-02-25: C++ now slightly faster). Shortcomings: win came from libstdc++ std::regex vs Rust regex crate and hand-written scanning (library, not language), C++ flags unstated and bench binaries not committed, single input file, baseline later fixed for a correctness bug, 0 stars. Not a duplicate.

tier_reason: The 0.3.0 release notes list 'Compared to GNU' speedups (sort 3.72x/1.46x, base64 1.20x, expand 1.80x, unexpand 1.50x, nl 1.57x, fold 1.19x, uniq -c 1.13x) with no hardware, input, GNU version or build profile; Phoronix and heise relay the project's figures rather than measuring (snippet only), so first-party tier C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 0.3.0 release notes (dated 24 October on the page; year not shown), 'Compared to GNU': sort 3.72x faster for regular sorting and 1.46x faster for numeric sorting, base64 1.20x faster, expand 1.80x faster, unexpand 1.50x faster, nl 1.57x faster, fold 1.19x faster, uniq -c 1.13x faster. The same notes' changelog says 'fold: improve the performances - now same as GNU', contradicting the 1.19x highlight. Release 0.11.0 (31 Aug) adds join '2.5x faster than GNU', attributed in the notes to skipping the locale comparison. Releases 0.8.0, 0.9.0, 0.10.0 and 0.12.0 carry no GNU-relative figures.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the comparisons. Repository [profile.release] uses lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1, panic = "abort"; GNU coreutils version and build flags unknown.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 24.2k stars, 2.1k forks; used by default in Ubuntu 25.10 (docs/src/performance.md)
corrections.caveats: No numbers in the README; the only figures are release-note highlights with no hardware, build profile, input size, locale or GNU version, so they cannot be reproduced from the page. docs/src/performance.md and src/uu/sort/BENCHMARKING.md give hyperfine recipes (and warn that locale matters a lot for sort) but no results; the in-tree CodSpeed/Divan benches compare uutils with itself, not GNU. base64 speed comes from the base64-simd crate (SIMD library, Cargo.toml), sort uses rayon, and the 0.11.0 join gain is attributed to skipping the locale comparison, so equal-work comparisons with GNU are not established. Search snippets (Phoronix, September 2025; not opened) reported Ubuntu 25.10 regressions: cksum up to 17x slower than GNU on some large files and sort never finishing on very large single-line files. A conference demo reported by an earlier search snippet showed a debug build only 1.45x faster than GNU sort and a release build about 6x (not verified here).

notes: Large, notable project; claim is first-party release-note highlights only, tier C. Shortcomings: no methodology (hardware, inputs, locale, GNU version), fold figure self-contradictory, base64 win from base64-simd SIMD crate and join win from skipping locale comparison (not same work or not language-level), some utilities reported slower than GNU (cksum up to 17x, snippet only). Not a language-level claim.
